lead: Natural language processing is the work of turning human text or speech into a structure another program can use: a label, a tree, a translation, a spoken reply. A bank wants to know whether a customer message is a complaint or a request. A student wants a Hindi sentence in English. Both need the same first move: take the raw input, find the units, and attach structure and meaning to them. NLP exists because language is the easiest way for people to give instructions and the hardest way to give them to a machine. It is used in search, translation, banking chatbots, review analysis and voice assistants.
prereq: You need only basic programming comfort; the language layers are introduced in levels of language analysis.

sections.h3: From hand-written rules to learned vectors

blocks.text: NLP is the field that builds programs which read or write human language. The input is text or speech. The output is a structure another program can use: a label, a tree, a translation, a short answer, a probability.

The work splits into two halves. Natural language understanding (NLU) goes from text to meaning. Natural language generation (NLG) goes from meaning to text. A rail enquiry chatbot needs both: it must read "when does the 6:40 to Tambaram leave" and then write a reply. Some syllabi use the single word NLP for the pair.
The field moved through three eras. They overlap, and none of them died.

items: Rules era. Linguists wrote grammars and dictionaries by hand, and the program checked the sentence against those patterns. It worked on clean, narrow text and broke on anything unexpected.

Statistical era. From the 1990s, text collections called corpora grew large enough to count. Instead of asking a linguist, the system estimated probabilities from counts: which word follows which, which tag fits which word. See Unit 2, N-gram Models.

Neural era. Words become vectors learned from data, and large pretrained models are fine-tuned on a small labelled set for each task. See Unit 5 for embeddings and Unit 6 for transformers. The gain is less hand-written rules and more generalisation; the cost is more data and compute.

blocks.text: Each item below is one task, not a separate field.

items: Spam filtering. A mail is labelled spam or not spam from its words and headers. This is binary text classification.
Machine translation. A sentence in one language becomes a sentence in another. See Unit 6.
Sentiment on product reviews. A review is labelled positive, negative or neutral. Sellers on Indian e-commerce sites read these at scale.
Search. A query is matched to documents and the documents are ranked by relevance. See Unit 6, information retrieval.
Chatbots for banking and rail enquiry. A fixed set of intents is recognised, then a template or a database lookup produces the reply.
Voice assistants. Speech is transcribed to text, NLP handles the text, and text-to-speech speaks the answer. See Unit 7.
Résumé screening. A CV is parsed into name, degree, skills and years of experience, then matched to a job description.

blocks.text: Ambiguity is the central difficulty. The same string carries more than one reading, and the reader must pick using context.

Lexical ambiguity: one word, several senses. "Bank" is a river edge or a money institution. "Bat" is a cricket bat or an animal. The fix needs surrounding words. See Unit 4, word sense disambiguation.

Syntactic ambiguity: one word sequence, two structures. In "She saw the man with the binoculars", the phrase "with the binoculars" attaches to "saw" (she used them) or to "the man" (he carried them). Parsing and attachment are covered in Unit 3.

Semantic ambiguity: the structure is fixed but the meaning of the whole is not. "Every student read a book" can mean one particular book for all students, or a possibly different book for each; the scope of "a book" changes. A different case is "The chicken is ready to eat": who does the eating changes, so it is an argument-structure ambiguity in "eat", not a fixed-structure semantic one. Selectional restrictions are covered in Unit 4.

Pragmatic ambiguity: the words are clear, the intended act is not. "Can you pass the salt?" asks about ability on paper; in a kitchen it is a request. Pragmatics is covered in levels of language analysis.
Systems rarely resolve these fully. Real pipelines carry several readings forward and let later evidence score them.

sections.h3: Beyond ambiguity: language variety, data and evaluation

blocks.text: Creativity and novel words. People coin words such as "selfie" and "upskilling", and they invent hashtags. A model trained on old text meets these as unknowns. Subword units help, but the first sighting is still a guess.
Code-mixing. Hinglish switches language inside one sentence: "kal meeting cancel hai". A word-level model trained on English sees noise, and the morphology rules of neither language apply cleanly.

Spelling variation on social media. "gud mrng", "plzz", doubled letters, dropped vowels. Standard dictionaries fail. Edit distance helps, as in spelling correction and minimum edit distance, but a deliberate misspelling and a typo look alike.

Rich morphology and free word order. Hindi, Tamil, Telugu and many other Indian languages carry case and agreement in suffixes and reorder arguments freely. English-shaped features lose this information. See morphology and finite-state transducers and tokenization.

Scarce labelled data. Raw text is easy to collect. Labelled data, meaning sentiment tags, parse trees or named entities, needs trained annotators and money. Most Indian languages have far less than English, so transfer from a high-resource language is common.

Evaluation. One sentence can have two correct translations, so a single accuracy number hides the truth. Test sets must be documented, and two scores may be compared only on the same split. See building corpora.

spec.aria: Four cards. Each card shows one sentence that branches into two readings: bank as river edge or money place; visiting relatives as relatives who visit or the act of visiting; pass the salt as a question or a request; with the binoculars attached to saw or to the man.

examples.question: Name the type of ambiguity in each sentence. (a) "He sat by the bank." (b) "Visiting relatives can be troublesome." (c) "Can you pass the salt?" (d) "She saw the man with the binoculars."
steps: (a) The word "bank" has a river-edge sense and a money sense. One word, two senses, so the ambiguity is lexical.
(b) "Visiting relatives" can be a noun phrase (relatives who visit) or a verb with its object (the act of visiting relatives). One string, two structures, so the ambiguity is syntactic.
(c) The form is a yes/no question about ability. Said at a dinner table it is a request to pass the salt. The words are clear and the act is not, so the ambiguity is pragmatic.
(d) The phrase "with the binoculars" can attach to "saw" (she used them) or to "the man" (he carried them). The words are unambiguous; the attachment site is not, so the ambiguity is syntactic.

traps: "NLP means machine translation." Translation is one application; the field also covers tagging, parsing, classification and generation.
"NLP began with deep learning." The rules era and the statistical era came first; deep learning is the third era, not the origin.
Mixing lexical and syntactic ambiguity. Lexical is one word with two senses; syntactic is one word string with two structures.
Treating a question form as a question in use. "Can you pass the salt?" is a request, so the label is pragmatic.
Assuming an English score transfers. A model good on English Wikipedia text is not automatically good on Hinglish tweets or Tamil news.

quiz.q: Define NLP and name its two halves.
quiz.a: NLP builds programs that read or write human language and output usable structure. The halves are NLU (text to meaning) and NLG (meaning to text).

quiz.q: Name the three eras of NLP in order and the main resource each one used.
quiz.a: Rules era used hand-written grammars and dictionaries; statistical era used counts from corpora; neural era uses vectors learned from data and pretrained models.

quiz.q: Why did the statistical era depend on corpora?
quiz.a: The method estimates probabilities from observed counts, so it needs a large fixed body of real text. Without a corpus there is nothing to count, and the estimates are the model.

quiz.q: Classify the ambiguity: (i) "a light bag" versus "a light switch"; (ii) "The chicken is ready to eat"; (iii) "Flying planes can be dangerous".
quiz.a: (i) Lexical: "light" means low weight or a lamp. (ii) Argument-structure ambiguity in "eat": the chicken may be the eater or the thing eaten, so who fills the eater role changes; it is not a fixed-structure semantic case. (iii) Syntactic: "flying planes" is a noun phrase (planes that fly) or a verb with object (the act of flying them).

quiz.q: Why does code-mixing such as Hinglish hurt a word-level model more than a spelling mistake does?
quiz.a: A spelling mistake leaves the word recognisable to a close match. Code-mixing swaps in words from a second language inside the same sentence, so the vocabulary, the morphology and often the word order all shift at once, and a model trained on one language has no matching evidence. Hinglish is usually typed in Roman script, so the script may stay the same while the language changes; script mixing, where Devanagari and Latin characters appear together, is an extra problem on top of that.

quiz.q: A team reports 92% accuracy on sentiment analysis. Give two reasons the number may not hold on new data.
quiz.a: The test split may come from the same source as training, so a new domain such as tweets or Hinglish reviews shifts the vocabulary. Also, a label set that ignores neutral reviews or sarcasm can inflate the score on the reported set only. Scores compare only on the same documented split.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern systems push most of the work into subword units and multilingual pretrained models, which soften the unknown-word and code-mixing problems without removing them. Indian-language corpora and benchmarks are an active area, and low-resource transfer is the usual practical answer. Evaluation has become its own research topic now that one prompt can produce many acceptable outputs. Search next for multilingual pretrained models, subword tokenization, and Indian-language NLP benchmarks.
